statement: An equilateral triangle tile is split into four smaller equilateral triangles by joining the midpoints of its sides. Each small triangle is painted red, yellow or blue; colours may repeat. Two tiles count as the same if one can be turned in its plane to look exactly like the other; flipping is not allowed. How many different tiles are there?

choices.misconception: I grouped the colourings in threes but left out the 9 tiles whose three corner triangles share one colour.
I divided all $3^4 = 81$ colourings by the 3 turns, but the 9 tiles with three matching corners look the same after every turn.
I also counted a tile and its mirror image as the same, but flipping over is not allowed.
I counted every way to paint the four triangles and did not treat turned copies as the same.

hints: Which small triangle stays in place when the tile is turned?
A turn moves the three corner triangles round in a cycle. Most colourings have three different turned copies, but some look the same after every turn: count those separately.
The middle triangle never moves. There are $3^4 = 81$ colourings. In 9 of them the three corners share a colour, and such a tile is unchanged by turning; the other 72 fall into groups of 3.

solutions.reliable: The middle triangle stays in place, and a turn through a third of a full turn moves the three corner triangles round a cycle. There are $3^4 = 81$ colourings in all. If the three corners have the same colour (3 choices), the tile looks the same after every turn; with 3 choices for the middle this gives 9 tiles, each in a group of its own. Any other colouring changes under both turns, so it has exactly three different turned copies, and the other $81 - 9 = 72$ colourings give $72 \div 3 = 24$ tiles. In total $9 + 24 = 33$. The transferable idea: when counting up to turning, count the colourings that a turn leaves unchanged separately before dividing.
solutions.elegant: Burnside's lemma: average the number of colourings that each turn leaves unchanged. Doing nothing fixes all 81, and each of the other two turns fixes the 9 with matching corners, so the count is $(81 + 9 + 9) \div 3 = 33$.

whyOnTest: Dividing by the number of turns only works for objects with no symmetry of their own, so the exceptions must be counted on their own.
